[&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h2","h2-0",{"children":"Queen Mary: The Flame of Resistance in the Danish West Indies"}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"Mary Thomas (c. 1848 – 1905), immortalized in history as \"Queen Mary,\" is one of the most revered figures in the labor history of the Caribbean. A central leader of the 1878 St. Croix labor revolt known as the \"Fireburn,\" her legacy is a testament to the enduring struggle for justice, dignity, and fair labor practices in the post-emancipation era. Emerging from the harsh realities of plantation life in the Danish West Indies (now the U.S. Virgin Islands), Queen Mary transformed from a laborer into a legendary symbol of resistance against colonial oppression and economic exploitation."}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"The Post-Emancipation Reality"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":"To understand the significance of Mary Thomas, one must understand the context of the Danish West Indies in the late 19th century. Although slavery was officially abolished in the colony in 1848—precipitated by a massive uprising led by figures like John Gottlieb (General Buddhoe)—the realities of freedom for the Black population were severely constrained. The colonial government instituted the Labor Act of 1849, a deeply oppressive system designed to maintain the plantation economy by binding workers to the land."}],"\n",["$","p","p-2",{"children":"Under this system, workers were required to sign annual contracts on October 1st, known as \"Contract Day.\" They were subjected to fixed, starvation-level wages, harsh working conditions, and severe restrictions on their mobility. The pass system effectively made it illegal for laborers to leave their plantations or seek better employment without the explicit permission of the estate owners. For thirty years, this system of indentured servitude bred deep resentment and a simmering anger among the laboring class."}],"\n","$L9","\n","$La","\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b"]}]]}],"$L1c","$L1d",false]}],"$L1e"]}]

8:["$","$L1f",null,{"children":["$","$20",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@21"}]}]
9:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Early Life of Mary Thomas"}]
a:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"Details about Mary Thomas's early life are relatively sparse, a common reality for working-class individuals and women of color in colonial records. It is believed she was born in Antigua around 1848, the very year slavery ended in the Danish territories. Sometime in the 1860s, she migrated to St. Croix, joining the workforce on the island's sugar plantations."}]
b:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"Before the events of 1878, records indicate she worked on various estates and had several children. She was known to be a woman of strong character, having been previously arrested for minor acts of defiance—a precursor to her future role as a revolutionary leader. Her life was defined by the grueling physical labor of the cane fields and the daily humiliations of a racially stratified and economically exploitative society."}]
c:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"Queen Mary, ah where you gon' go burn? / Queen Mary, ah where you gon' go burn? / Don't ask me nothin' t'all / Just give me the match and oil / Bassin Jailhouse, ah there the money dey.\"\n— Traditional Virgin Islands folk song commemorating the Fireburn."}],"\n"]}]
d:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The Eruption of the Fireburn"}]
e:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"The tension reached a breaking point on October 1, 1878. As laborers gathered in the town of Frederiksted for Contract Day, rumors circulated that the colonial authorities would deny their demands for higher wages and better living conditions. Furthermore, the workers' request to freely leave the island to seek better opportunities was vehemently opposed by the planters."}]
f:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"When their demands were flatly rejected, the accumulated anger of three decades erupted. The workers began to riot, targeting the symbols of their oppression: the sugar plantations and the colonial infrastructure. This uprising became known as the \"Fireburn,\" the largest labor revolt in the history of the Danish colonial empire."}]
10:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"The Three Queens"}]
11:["$","p","p-7",{"children":"During the Fireburn, leadership naturally emerged from the ranks of the workers. Among the most prominent leaders were three women: Mary Thomas, Axeline \"Agnes\" Elizabeth Salomon, and Matilde McBean. The laborers bestowed the title of \"Queen\" upon them, a title that held deep cultural significance, rooted in African traditions and the social structures of Caribbean societies. The \"Queens\" were not only strategic leaders but also moral authorities who inspired the crowds and directed the course of the uprising."}]
12:["$","p","p-8",{"children":"Queen Mary, in particular, became the face of the rebellion. Armed with a cane knife and a torch, she was reportedly at the forefront of the demonstrations. The revolt lasted for several days, during which over 50 plantations—more than half the island's agricultural infrastructure—were set ablaze. The sky over St. Croix glowed red with the fires of resistance."}]
13:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a2/I_Am_Queen_Mary.jpg","alt":"I Am Queen Mary statue"}]}]
14:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Suppression, Imprisonment, and Exile"}]
15:["$","p","p-10",{"children":"The Danish colonial authorities responded with overwhelming military force. Troops were dispatched to crush the rebellion, resulting in the deaths of over a hundred laborers. Hundreds more were arrested in the brutal crackdown that followed."}]
16:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"Mary Thomas, along with Queen Agnes and Queen Matilda, was captured and brought before a military tribunal. Recognized as the instigators of the Fireburn, they were initially sentenced to death for their roles in the uprising. However, due to various political considerations and perhaps a fear of turning them into even greater martyrs, their sentences were commuted to life imprisonment with hard labor."}]
17:["$","p","p-12",{"children":"In 1882, the colonial authorities, deeming the presence of the Queens too dangerous on the island, transferred them to Denmark. They were incarcerated in the Women's Prison in Christianshavn, Copenhagen. The sight of these Caribbean women in a European prison was a stark physical manifestation of the colonial relationship. Despite their harsh circumstances, their spirit remained unbroken. Eventually, in 1887, they were returned to St. Croix to serve the remainder of their sentences in Christiansted. Mary Thomas lived out her final years on the island, passing away in 1905."}]
18:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Legacy: I Am Queen Mary"}]
19:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"For over a century, the story of Queen Mary was kept alive primarily through oral history, folk songs, and the deeply held cultural memory of the Virgin Islands people. She became an icon of resistance, an embodiment of the strength and resilience of Caribbean women."}]
1a:["$","p","p-14",{"children":["In recent years, her legacy has received profound international recognition. In 2018, to mark the centennial of the sale of the Danish West Indies to the United States, a monumental public sculpture titled ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"I Am Queen Mary"}]," was unveiled in Copenhagen. Created collaboratively by Virgin Islands artist La Vaughn Belle and Danish artist Jeannette Ehlers, the striking statue sits in front of the West Indian Warehouse. It depicts Queen Mary seated majestically in a wicker chair—reminiscent of the iconic photograph of Huey P. Newton—holding a torch in one hand and a cane knife in the other."]}]
1b:["$","p","p-15",{"children":"This monument, Denmark's first public statue of a Black woman, forces a confrontation with the nation's colonial past and honors the heroism of those who fought against it. Queen Mary’s life story—from a laborer in the cane fields to a leader of a massive rebellion, and finally to a global symbol of anti-colonial resistance—demonstrates the profound impact of grassroots activism. She remains a powerful reminder that the fight for labor rights and human dignity in the Caribbean was forged in fire and led by those with the most to lose."}]
1c:["$","$L22",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Queen Mary (Mary Thomas)","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/queen-mary"}]
1d:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"Mary Thomas, known as 'Queen Mary,' was a primary leader of the 1878 'Fireburn' labor revolt in St. Croix, the largest uprising in Danish colonial history. By organizing and leading plantation workers to demand fair wages and the abolition of oppressive labor laws, she struck a critical blow against the exploitative post-emancipation plantation economy. Her courageous leadership not only forced colonial authorities to eventually reform labor conditions but also enshrined her as an enduring cultural icon of resistance, labor rights, and female empowerment in the U.S. Virgin Islands and the broader Caribbean."}]]}]
